spec.full_target:
Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n. The finite energy E:(0,∞)→ℝ is differentiable at every t>0 and E'(t)=0. In particular E(b)=E(a) for all a,b>0, with exactly the normalization E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n} (|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²) dx and no assertion at time zero.

hypotheses.statement: u is jointly smooth on the open set ℝ^n×(0,∞).

For every pair of real times 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact set C⊂ℝ^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and every r∈[s,t].

definitions.type: coordinate differentiation and Euclidean notation convention on the given open domain
definitions.definition: On ℝ^n and ℝ^m use the standard Euclidean inner product v·w=∑_k v_k w_k and norm |v|=(v·v)^(1/2). Spatial Lebesgue measure dx is the product of the n ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in the standard coordinates. For any function on ℝ^n×(0,∞), ∂_{x_j} means its componentwise derivative in spatial coordinate j (1≤j≤n), and ∂_t its componentwise time derivative, where these derivatives exist. In particular u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t(∂_t u), and ∂_{x_jx_j}u=∂_{x_j}(∂_{x_j}u). For scalar functions the same conventions apply. D_xu denotes the matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and its squared Frobenius norm is ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|². Smooth means derivatives of every finite order exist and are continuous on the stated open domain. An integral without a displayed measure is the Lebesgue integral; integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value (or norm).

For every x∈ℝ^n and t>0, e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|².

After integrability has been established, define E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n} e(x,t) dx for every t>0. Differentiability and E'(t) mean the ordinary two-sided real derivative on this open time interval, equivalently the derivative of any local extension near t.

Let A be a measurable space with a measure μ, and G a normed additive commutative group and real normed vector space. Let I be an index type and l a countably generated filter on I. Given F:I→A→G, f:A→G and b:A→ℝ, assume (i) eventually in l, F(i) is μ-a.e. strongly measurable; (ii) eventually in l, |F(i,x)|≤b(x) for μ-a.e. x; (iii) b is μ-integrable; (iv) for μ-a.e. x, F(i,x) tends along l to f(x). Then ∫ F(i,x) dμ tends along l to ∫ f(x) dμ.

locals.declaration: Choose a real a with u_tt(x,t)−Δ_xu(x,t)=a u(x,t) by H005.

argument.text: Fix x∈ℝ^n and t>0. By H002 all the coordinate curves and derivatives used here are differentiable near this interior point. H004 gives u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 for r near t. Apply M007 over ℝ with both curves r↦u(x,r) and both derivatives u_t(x,t). The derivative of the constant right side is zero, while that of the left side is 2u(x,t)·u_t(x,t). Thus u·u_t=0 at (x,t). The same argument along any spatial coordinate gives u·∂_{x_j}u=0. These identities hold throughout the open domain.

produces.statement: Throughout ℝ^n×(0,∞), u·u_t=0 and u·∂_{x_j}u=0 for each 1≤j≤n.

argument.text: Choose a from H005 at (x,t). Using F001, u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=u_t·(a u)=a(u_t·u)=0, without differentiating a. For completeness retain the explicit equation from the supplied proof. Differentiate the identities u·u_t=0 and u·∂_{x_j}u=0 once more along their respective coordinate curves. M007 gives u·u_tt=−|u_t|² and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting u_tt−Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 gives a=∑_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². The same algebra applies to every scalar satisfying the normality equation, not just the chosen witness.

produces.statement: At the arbitrary (x,t), u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0, and for every α∈ℝ, if u_tt−Δ_xu=αu then α=∑_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|².

argument.text: By H002, derivatives of every order are continuous; finite inner products and finite sums of their components are smooth, so e is smooth. To identify its time derivative, apply M008 over ℝ to u locally at (x,t), with order 2. One may extend u arbitrarily outside the open domain: all derivative statements are local and the point has a neighborhood wholly in the domain. Evaluate symmetry on the time direction and the jth spatial coordinate direction. These evaluations of the second Fréchet derivative are respectively ∂_t∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t, hence they agree. Apply M007 to the time curves u_t and u_t, and to ∂_{x_j}u and itself for each index; differentiating the finite sum defining e now gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. It is continuous by H002. F001 and F002 and these identities hold for arbitrary x,t; universal introduction proves the full output.

argument.text: Choose L from F002 and set R=max(1,L+1), Q=[−R,R]^n. Then R>0 and for x∈C every coordinate satisfies |x_j|≤|x|≤L<R. Thus C⊂(−R,R)^n=int Q. For the coordinate product Lebesgue measure its measure is the finite product ∏_{j=1}^n(2R)=(2R)^n<∞.

argument.text: The set (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open, since compact C is closed in Euclidean space. There u is identically the fixed q by F001. At every point of this open set all positive-order coordinate derivatives vanish: the first derivative is the limit of zero difference quotients in a neighborhood, and repetition proves the assertion at every finite order. H002 gives continuity of all derivatives everywhere on the time-domain. Therefore, at any r∈int J, every spatial function in the output's list is continuous and zero off C; its nonzero set has closure contained in the closed compact C. Apply M005 to each of these functions. This proves all their integrability claims, including e(·,t0), e_t and every product used later. Equivalently, each is bounded in absolute value on Q by M006 and has absolute integral at most that bound times (2R)^n.

N002 proves |e_t|≤B on the corresponding space-time box. N001 gives that r↦e(x,r) is differentiable at each point of this interval with derivative e_t(x,r). For every x∈Q and 0<|h|<η, apply M004 on this real convex interval with endpoints t0,t0+h. It yields |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Outside Q both densities are zero by N002, since C⊂int Q. argument.text: Define F(h,x) as the difference quotient for 0<|h|<η and zero otherwise. For these small nonzero h, its spatial section is continuous by N001 and is integrable by N002 and linearity of integrability. Hence it is a.e. strongly measurable. At every fixed x the difference quotients tend, as h→0 through h≠0, to e_t(x,t0), by N001. F001 and F002 give an integrable bound for the punctured germ. Apply M001 to Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n, scalar codomain ℝ, parameter h∈ℝ with filter 𝓝[≠]0, F as just defined, f(x)=e_t(x,t0), and bound bnd. The filter is countably generated, with the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k as a countable neighborhood basis. Consequently ∫F(h,x)dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx along that filter.

produces.statement: As h→0 with h≠0, ∫_{ℝ^n} F(h,x) dx tends to ∫_{ℝ^n} e_t(x,t0) dx.

argument.text: N002 discharges the guard for E and gives integrability of e(·,t0+h) and e(·,t0) at the nearby positive times, as well as of e_t(·,t0). For 0<|h|<η, linearity of the integral gives ∫F(h,x)dx=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. F003 is therefore exactly the difference-quotient criterion for differentiability of this finite real-valued E: E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substitute the full e_t identity from N001. Every summand is integrable by N002. H002 ensures the derivative notation has its usual classical meaning on the open time-domain. Since t0 was arbitrary, this proves the full differentiation assertion.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and an index 1≤j≤n. Choose compatible C,R from N002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n and g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). H002 makes g smooth. N002 gives g=0 off C and C⊂int Q, so g vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of Q (the open complement of C contains that boundary). Apply M007 along the jth coordinate to u_t and ∂_{x_j}u at time t0. This gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. Each term is continuous and integrable by N002.

produces.statement: g is smooth, zero near ∂Q, and ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(·,t0)+u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,t0). All three functions in this equality are integrable and vanish outside C.

argument.text: For each fixed choice of the remaining n−1 coordinates in [−R,R], consider the scalar function of x_j obtained by restricting g to that coordinate line. It is smooth on ℝ, including both endpoints −R and R. Its derivative is continuous and hence integrable on this compact interval, and the function has zero value at both endpoints because these points lie on ∂Q, outside C. M002 therefore gives ∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g dx_j=0. Use M003 with the jth restricted Lebesgue coordinate as the inner factor and the product of the other restricted coordinates as the outer factor. The integrand on Q is integrable by F001 (also continuous and bounded on a finite-measure box), and both factor measures are finite, hence s-finite. This yields ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=0. This product decomposition is just the standard coordinate product defining dx: regroup the finite coordinates and put the jth coordinate last; finite coordinate permutations preserve that product measure. If n=1 there are no remaining coordinates and no Fubini step is needed: the FTC equality already is the required box integral. Endpoints do not affect the Lebesgue interval integral since singletons have zero measure.

All terms of F001 vanish outside Q by N002, since C⊂int Q. Thus their integrals over Q equal their whole-space integrals. Integrate the equality in F001 and use F002 and linearity for the integrable summands: 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Symmetry of the real dot product and subtraction give precisely the asserted integration-by-parts identity, including finiteness of both sides. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the output.

argument.text: Fix t0>0. N002 proves integrability of e(·,t0) and all the products below and discharges the guard for the actual finite E. Sum the integration-by-parts identity N004 over the finite spatial indices and substitute it to obtain E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·u_tt dx−2∑_{j=1}^n ∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx. argument.text: For the constancy asserted in the supplied proof, fix any a,b>0. On S=[min(a,b),max(a,b)] all times are positive. Substituting D003 and D004 shows the exact normalization in P, with no factor 1/2; all times used are strictly positive and no value or assertion at time zero was introduced.
